messages.author: 0d1597ed161c7be7
messages.subject: GAM
parts:
Thanks!

I've seen that and other R links and found a free pdf of the full text of Wood's 2006 book "GAMs in R" but it's quite thick, I'm still trying to make sense of it. Maybe that website will be faster for my purposes.

Attached and below is Neil Willits's advice and my response if anyone's interested!

---------- Forwarded message ----------

This is wonderful Neil.


Regarding potential predictors:

1.       I haven’t found much data on groundwater chloride. I’ll make a last quick effort to contact the right people at USGS, NV govs and UNR. In the meantime I’ll move on without it, since the correlations with arsenic are fairly weak anyway (Welch and Lico 1998).

2.       There are other potential predictors like soil particle size for which I’ve found rough estimates at all locations, but so far they don’t look too promising either. So again, I’m thinking I should learn how to run the model now with the few variables I already have at all well locations, and then if time permits hopefully I could quickly go back and see if other variables improve predictions.

3.       As you suggested, depth of well is known to be an important predictor, but it’s unknown for ~40% of wells, including those of health study participants that we want to estimate. So I agree we should make a “depth-free” model, at least for starters.

4.       That leaves only the coordinates, surface elevation, and river inputs.

Thanks again for being my “lifeline” away from Berkeley!

Dave 530 416 0418



2014-09-03 13:51 GMT-07:00 Neil Willits <nhwi...@ucdavis.edu>:

Dave,

        Here's what I came up with in terms of a summary of our meeting this morning.  Please check it over for accuracy/completeness and let me know if there are important details that need to be corrected or fleshed out.  Otherwise, good luck with the analysis, and let me know if you get stuck, in case you want to meet again.  Bear in mind though that I've not done this type of analysis in R, so I'm not apt to be all that helpful for questions dealing specifically with R.

                                        -Neil Willits
                                         Department of Statistics.
